{"ALGEBRA/ch1/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A group captures the essence of symmetry and reversible operation — the same four axioms describe integer addition, matrix multiplication, and Rubik's-cube moves. It's the starting point of modern algebra.

Group
A set G with an operation ∗ is a group if: (1) closure, (2) associativity, (3) an identity e with e∗a = a∗e = a, and (4) every a has an inverse a⁻¹ with a∗a⁻¹ = e. If ∗ is commutative, G is abelian.
WORKED EXAMPLE — examples and non-examples

(ℤ, +) is a group: identity 0, inverse of a is −a, abelian.

(ℤ, ×) is NOT a group: 2 has no integer multiplicative inverse.

(ℤₙ, +) — integers mod n — is a group of order n.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Four axioms, all required. A set with an associative operation and identity but missing inverses is a MONOID, not a group (e.g. ℕ under +).

📊 FIGURE — A Cayley table wears the axioms on its sleeve
ℤ₄ under addition: every cell stays in {0,1,2,3} (closure); the 0 row/column repeats the headers (identity); every row contains 0 somewhere (inverses exist); and each row is a perfect shuffle of the elements — the Latin-square property every group table has.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch1/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Subgroups are groups sitting inside groups; the order of an element (how many times you apply it to return to identity) reveals deep structure — and leads straight to Lagrange's theorem.

Subgroup test
A nonempty subset H ⊆ G is a subgroup if it is closed under the operation and under inverses (equivalently: a,b ∈ H ⇒ a∗b⁻¹ ∈ H).
Order of an element
The order of a ∈ G is the smallest positive n with aⁿ = e (or ∞ if none). The order of the GROUP is |G|, its number of elements.
WORKED EXAMPLE — order of an element

In (ℤ₆, +), find the order of 2.

2, 2+2=4, 4+2=6≡0. So 3·2 ≡ 0 (mod 6) and no smaller multiple is 0. The order of 2 is 3.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Element order (smallest n with aⁿ = e) is different from group order (|G|). Lagrange's theorem ties them together: element order divides |G|.

📊 FIGURE — ℤ₆: one generator walks the whole group
Starting at 0 and repeatedly adding the generator 1 visits every element before cycling home — that single-orbit structure is what \"cyclic\" means. Generators are exactly the elements coprime to 6 (1 and 5); starting from 2 you would only ever see {0, 2, 4}.
📊 FIGURE — what carries down to a subgroup
🎯 EXAM TIP
Every subgroup of an abelian group is abelian. Commutativity is a statement about elements, and a subgroup's elements are already elements of G, so the property comes for free. The implication runs one way only: S₃ has abelian subgroups but is not itself abelian.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch1/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Cyclic groups — generated by a single element — are the simplest and most fundamental groups; every group of prime order is cyclic, and they classify all finitely generated abelian groups.

Cyclic group
G is cyclic if G = ⟨g⟩ = {gⁿ : n ∈ ℤ} for some generator g. (ℤ, +) = ⟨1⟩ is infinite cyclic; (ℤₙ, +) is cyclic of order n.
WORKED EXAMPLE — generators of ℤ₆

(ℤ₆, +): 1 generates everything (1,2,3,4,5,0), so 1 is a generator; 5 also is.

The generators of ℤₙ are exactly the elements coprime to n. For n=6: gcd(k,6)=1 gives k = 1, 5. So there are φ(6) = 2 generators.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Not every element generates the whole group. In ℤ₆, the element 2 only generates {0,2,4} (a subgroup of order 3). Generators are the ones coprime to n.

📊 FIGURE — ℤ₆: one generator walks the whole group
Starting at 0 and repeatedly adding the generator 1 visits every element before cycling home — that single-orbit structure is what \"cyclic\" means. Generators are exactly the elements coprime to 6 (1 and 5); starting from 2 you would only ever see {0, 2, 4}.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch2/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Lagrange's theorem — the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group — is the single most-used counting fact in group theory, constraining what subgroups and element orders can exist.

Coset
For subgroup H ≤ G and g ∈ G, the left coset is gH = {gh : h ∈ H}. Cosets partition G into equal-sized pieces, each of size |H|.
Lagrange's theorem
If G is finite and H ≤ G, then |H| divides |G|. The number of cosets, |G|/|H|, is the index [G:H].
WORKED EXAMPLE — consequences of Lagrange

A group of order 12 can only have subgroups of order 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (the divisors of 12).

Also, every element's order divides 12, and any group of prime order (say 7) has no nontrivial subgroups — hence is cyclic.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Lagrange says a subgroup's order MUST divide |G|, but the converse fails in general: a divisor of |G| need not have a subgroup of that order (A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6).

📊 FIGURE — Cosets slice the group into equal pieces
The subgroup H and its cosets aH, bH partition G: same size, no overlap, nothing missed. Counting the slices gives Lagrange instantly — |G| = |H| × (number of cosets), so |H| must divide |G|.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch2/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A homomorphism preserves the operation; an isomorphism is a perfect structural match. They let us say two groups are 'the same' and transport results between them.

Homomorphism
φ: G → H with φ(a∗b) = φ(a)∗φ(b). Its kernel = {g : φ(g) = e_H} is a (normal) subgroup of G; its image is a subgroup of H. φ is an isomorphism if it is also a bijection.
WORKED EXAMPLE — a homomorphism

φ: (ℤ, +) → (ℤₙ, +), φ(k) = k mod n, is a homomorphism: φ(a+b) = (a+b) mod n = φ(a)+φ(b).

Its kernel is the multiples of n, {..., −n, 0, n, 2n, ...}; its image is all of ℤₙ.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

A homomorphism is injective (one-to-one) exactly when its kernel is trivial ({e}). Checking the kernel is the standard way to test injectivity.

📊 FIGURE — A homomorphism preserves the multiplication table
Combine first then map, or map first then combine — you land in the same place: φ(a·b) = φ(a)∘φ(b). The kernel (everything sent to e′) measures how much φ collapses; trivial kernel means a faithful (injective) copy.
📊 FIGURE — free consequences of φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Deriving the two automatic properties

Identity. Since e = ee, applying φ gives

φ(e) = φ(ee) = φ(e)φ(e)

Multiplying both sides by φ(e)⁻¹ in H cancels one factor and leaves φ(e_G) = e_H.

Inverses. Now use that result:

φ(a)φ(a⁻¹) = φ(aa⁻¹) = φ(e) = e_H

So φ(a⁻¹) is the inverse of φ(a): φ(a⁻¹) = φ(a)⁻¹.

Both fall straight out of the defining property. Injectivity and surjectivity do not — they are extra hypotheses, which is why the words monomorphism, epimorphism and isomorphism exist to name them.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Any group homomorphism automatically satisfies φ(e_G) = e_H and φ(a⁻¹) = φ(a)⁻¹. Injectivity and surjectivity are not automatic — the trivial map sending everything to e_H is a perfectly good homomorphism and is neither.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch2/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Normal subgroups are exactly the ones you can 'divide by' to form a quotient group G/N — the algebraic analogue of modular arithmetic, and the setting of the First Isomorphism Theorem.

Normal subgroup
N ⊴ G if gNg⁻¹ = N for all g (left and right cosets coincide). Then the cosets form the quotient group G/N under (aN)(bN) = abN.
First Isomorphism Theorem
For a homomorphism φ: G → H, G/ker(φ) ≅ image(φ). Quotient by the kernel recovers the image exactly.
WORKED EXAMPLE — a quotient group

ℤ/nℤ: take G = ℤ, N = nℤ (multiples of n). N is normal (ℤ is abelian), and the quotient ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤₙ — integers mod n.

This is the First Isomorphism Theorem applied to φ(k) = k mod n: ℤ/ker φ = ℤ/nℤ ≅ ℤₙ.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

In a non-abelian group, not every subgroup is normal — you need gNg⁻¹ = N. Only normal subgroups produce well-defined quotient groups. In abelian groups every subgroup is normal.

📊 FIGURE — Cosets slice the group into equal pieces
The subgroup H and its cosets aH, bH partition G: same size, no overlap, nothing missed. Counting the slices gives Lagrange instantly — |G| = |H| × (number of cosets), so |H| must divide |G|.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch3/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A ring has two operations (add and multiply) — the abstraction of the integers and polynomials. Refining to integral domains and fields captures when division and cancellation behave well.

Ring
(R, +, ·): an abelian group under +, associative under ·, with distributive laws. An integral domain is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 and NO zero divisors (ab = 0 ⇒ a = 0 or b = 0). A field is a commutative ring where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
WORKED EXAMPLE — zero divisors

In ℤ₆: 2 · 3 = 6 ≡ 0, yet 2 ≠ 0 and 3 ≠ 0. So 2 and 3 are ZERO DIVISORS, and ℤ₆ is NOT an integral domain.

But ℤ₅ has no zero divisors (5 is prime) — it's even a field.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

ℤₙ is an integral domain (and a field) exactly when n is PRIME. Composite n always has zero divisors (its factors).

📊 FIGURE — The algebra hierarchy, nested
Every field is an integral domain, and every integral domain is a commutative ring — each ring inward adds an axiom: no zero divisors, then multiplicative inverses. Placing a structure in the right ring of this diagram answers half of the definition questions.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch3/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Polynomial rings F[x] over a field behave like the integers: there's a division algorithm, a notion of primes (irreducibles), and unique factorization — the machinery behind coding theory and algebraic number theory.

Polynomial ring
F[x] is the ring of polynomials with coefficients in a field F. Division algorithm: for f, g ≠ 0 there are unique q, r with f = qg + r and deg r < deg g.
Factor theorem
a is a root of f (f(a) = 0) if and only if (x − a) divides f. A degree-n polynomial has at most n roots in a field.
WORKED EXAMPLE — factor theorem

f(x) = x² − 5x + 6 over ℝ. f(2) = 4 − 10 + 6 = 0, so (x − 2) is a factor.

Dividing: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). The roots 2, 3 correspond exactly to the factors.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The 'at most n roots' rule needs the coefficients to come from a FIELD (or integral domain). Over ℤₙ with n composite, a polynomial can have more roots than its degree.

📊 FIGURE — The algebra hierarchy, nested
Every field is an integral domain, and every integral domain is a commutative ring — each ring inward adds an axiom: no zero divisors, then multiplicative inverses. Placing a structure in the right ring of this diagram answers half of the definition questions.
"}, "ALGEBRA/ch3/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Finite fields (like ℤₚ) power modern cryptography and error-correcting codes. RSA, elliptic-curve crypto, and CDs all run on the algebra you've just built.

Finite field
ℤₚ (p prime) is a field with p elements; every nonzero element has an inverse. General finite fields have order pᵏ. Fermat's little theorem: aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p) for a ≢ 0.
WORKED EXAMPLE — modular inverse for crypto

In ℤ₇, find the inverse of 3. We need 3x ≡ 1 (mod 7). Testing: 3·5 = 15 ≡ 1. So 3⁻¹ = 5.

RSA relies on exactly this: computing modular inverses (of the encryption exponent modulo φ(n)) to build the decryption key.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Modular inverses exist only when the element is coprime to the modulus. In ℤₚ with p prime, every nonzero element qualifies — which is why fields (not just rings) are used in crypto.

📊 FIGURE — RSA in one diagram
Anyone may encrypt with the PUBLIC key (e, n); only the private d undoes it, because computing d requires the factors p, q of n — and factoring a 2048-bit n is infeasible. Signatures run the same math in reverse: encrypt with d, verify with e.
📊 FIGURE — finite fields in cryptography
🎯 EXAM TIP
AES performs its byte arithmetic in GF(2⁸), the 256-element finite field, because a byte has exactly 256 possible values. Addition in that field is plain XOR, and the field structure matters because MixColumns and the S-box require every nonzero byte to have a multiplicative inverse.
"}, "ALGEBRA/solving/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

In the cyclic group Zn (integers mod n under addition), the order of an element a is ord(a) = n / gcd(a, n). The element generates all of Zn exactly when gcd(a,n) = 1, so the number of generators of Zn is Euler's totient φ(n).

Modular arithmetic

Reduce after every operation. For multiplication, a·b mod n is the remainder of a·b divided by n. For powers, reduce step by step: 5² = 25 ≡ 4 (mod 7), then 5³ = 5·4 = 20 ≡ 6 (mod 7).

Permutations

The order of a permutation written as disjoint cycles is the lcm of the cycle lengths. Example: (1 2 3)(4 5) has order lcm(3,2) = 6. To compose permutations σ∘τ, apply the right factor τ first, then σ, tracking where each point lands.

Counting subgroups

Every subgroup of Zn is cyclic and there is exactly one subgroup for each divisor of n. So the number of subgroups equals the number of divisors of n. For Z12 the divisors are 1,2,3,4,6,12 — six subgroups.

Worked example: order of 4 in Z12 is 12 / gcd(4,12) = 12 / 4 = 3.

"}, "ALGEBRA/solving/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Lagrange's theorem: if H is a subgroup of a finite group G, then |H| divides |G|, and the number of cosets — the index [G:H] — is |G| / |H|. Example: a subgroup of order 6 in a group of order 24 has index 24/6 = 4.

Product groups

In Zm × Zn, the order of an element (a, b) is lcm( ord(a), ord(b) ), where each coordinate's order is computed in its own group. Example: (1,1) in Z4 × Z6 has order lcm(4, 6) = 12.

Euler's totient

For n = p₁^{a₁} · p₂^{a₂} ···, φ(n) = n · Π (1 − 1/pᵢ). Example: φ(36) = 36·(1 − 1/2)(1 − 1/3) = 36 · 1/2 · 2/3 = 12.

Unit group

U(n) is the group of integers mod n that are coprime to n, under multiplication, and |U(n)| = φ(n). A number a generates Zn iff gcd(a,n) = 1; its order is n/gcd(a,n).

Worked example: the index of the subgroup ⟨4⟩ = {0,4,8} in Z12 is 12 / 3 = 4.

"}, "ALGEBRA/solving_only/sim": {"body": "

"}, "ALGEBRA/solving2/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

In the additive group Zn, the order of an element a is given by n / gcd(a, n). For example, the order of 4 in Z12 is 12 / gcd(4,12) = 12/4 = 3.

Generators and subgroups

The number of generators of Zn equals Euler's totient φ(n), the count of integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n. Because Zn is cyclic, the number of subgroups equals the number of positive divisors of n — one subgroup for each divisor.

Modular arithmetic

To compute a product or power modulo m, reduce at each step. Example: 5^3 mod 7 = 125 mod 7 = 6, since 7·17 = 119 and 125 − 119 = 6.

Permutations

The order of a permutation written as disjoint cycles is the lcm of the cycle lengths. So the order of (1 2 3)(4 5) is lcm(3,2) = 6. To compose permutations στ (apply τ first, then σ), trace each point through τ and then through σ. For σ = (1 2 3), τ = (1 2): 1→2→3, 2→1→2, 3→3→1, giving (1 3).

"}, "ALGEBRA/solving2/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

Lagrange's theorem: if H is a subgroup of a finite group G, the index [G:H] — the number of distinct cosets — equals |G| / |H|. For |G| = 24 and |H| = 6, the index is 24/6 = 4.

Product groups

In Zm × Zn, the order of an element (a, b) is the lcm of the orders of its coordinates. The order of (1, 1) in Z4 × Z6 is lcm(4, 6) = 12.

Totient and units

Euler's φ(n) counts integers from 1 to n coprime to n. For a prime factorization, multiply n by (1 − 1/p) over each distinct prime p. So φ(24) = 24 · (1/2) · (2/3) = 8. The group of units U(n) has order |U(n)| = φ(n).

Generating and counting

An element a generates all of Zn exactly when gcd(a, n) = 1; otherwise the subgroup ⟨a⟩ has order n / gcd(a, n). The total number of subgroups of Zn equals the number of divisors of n.

The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.

Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition.
